expectedText:
PROBATE REFEREE AND THE INVENTORY AND APPRAISAL — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan Rivera · Morgan Lee

PURPOSE OF THIS PROBATE REFEREE AND INVENTORY-AND-APPRAISAL INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet states general facts about the statutory inventory-and-appraisal procedure set out in Probate Code Part 3 (commencing with § 8800) and the probate-referee appointment provisions in Probate Code Part 12 (commencing with § 400), as those provisions apply to the pending administration of Pat Morgan Rivera's estate before Superior Court of California in Alameda County, case number PRO-26-123456, in which Morgan Lee has been appointed personal representative. It describes the deadline for filing an inventory and appraisal, how a probate referee is appointed, which items the personal representative appraises directly and which items go to the referee, the duty to supplement the inventory for later-discovered property, and how the referee is compensated. It does not itself file any inventory and appraisal, does not select or appoint any probate referee, and does not advise Morgan Lee what to do about any specific item of estate property.

DUTY TO FILE AN INVENTORY AND APPRAISAL, AND THE FOUR-MONTH DEADLINE
Probate Code § 8800(a) requires a personal representative to file with the court clerk an inventory of the property to be administered in Pat Morgan Rivera's estate, together with an appraisal of that property, combined in a single document. Under § 8800(b), the inventory and appraisal must be filed within four months after letters are first issued to a general personal representative, though the court may allow further time as is reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case. Section 8800(c) permits the personal representative to file partial inventories and appraisals where appropriate, so long as all of them are filed before the four-month period (or any court-allowed extension) expires.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The personal representative shall file with the court clerk an inventory of property to be administered in the decedent’s estate together with an appraisal of property in the inventory. An inventory and appraisal shall be combined in a single document."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8800(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8800(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8800.)
  "The inventory and appraisal shall be filed within four months after letters are first issued to a general personal representative. The court may allow such further time for filing an inventory and appraisal as is reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8800(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8800(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8800.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only §8800(a)-(c). It does not address §8800(d), a separate requirement (added by a 1992 amendment) that the personal representative concurrently file a certification regarding whether a change-in-ownership statement under Revenue and Taxation Code § 480 has been filed with the county recorder or assessor for any California real property the decedent owned at death — that certification requirement is not independently verified or explained here. Nor does this clause address what counts as letters being 'first issued to a general personal representative' in cases involving a prior special administrator, or how the deadline interacts with an extension the court has already granted in a particular county.

HOW PROBATE REFEREES ARE APPOINTED FOR THE COUNTY
Probate Code § 400(a) requires the State Controller to appoint at least one person in each county to act as probate referee for that county. Section 400(b) addresses counties where too few qualified people are available: if there are fewer than three qualified applicants to serve in a county, the Controller may designate a probate referee from another county, or make an interim appointment, to serve until the vacancy is filled by a qualified applicant.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The Controller shall appoint at least one person in each county to act as a probate referee for the county."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 400(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 400(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=400.)
  "If there are fewer than three qualified applicants to serve in a county, the Controller may designate a probate referee from another county or make an interim appointment, to serve until the vacancy has been filled by a qualified applicant."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 400(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 400(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=400.)
  Known gap: This clause does not state how many probate referees the Controller has currently appointed for any particular county, nor whether a given county presently has fewer than three qualified applicants triggering the out-of-county-designation or interim-appointment provision in § 400(b) — that is a factual, county-specific condition this document does not independently verify. It also does not address how the personal representative selects among the referees a county does have, which is governed by a separate section not quoted in this clause.

QUALIFICATION REQUIREMENTS FOR APPOINTMENT AS A PROBATE REFEREE
Probate Code § 401(a) provides that appointment as a probate referee is made from among persons who have passed a qualification examination, and that a person who passes the examination remains eligible for appointment for five years from the date of the examination. Section 401(b) separately requires that appointment be made on the basis of merit, without regard to sex, race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, marital status, or political affiliation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Appointment shall be from among persons passing a qualification examination. A person who passes the examination is eligible for appointment for a period of five years from the date of the examination."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 401(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 401(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=401.)
  Known gap: Section 401 does not itself state how often the qualification examination is offered, who administers it, or what subject matter it covers — this clause does not independently research or verify those examination details. Nor does it address what happens if a person's five-year eligibility window under § 401(a) expires without appointment.

REQUIRED FORM AND CONTENTS OF THE INVENTORY AND APPRAISAL
Probate Code § 8802 requires that the inventory and appraisal separately list each item of Pat Morgan Rivera's estate property and state the fair market value of that item, as of the date of Pat Morgan Rivera's death, in monetary terms opposite the item. Section 8850(a) requires that the inventory — including any partial or supplemental inventories — include all property to be administered in Pat Morgan Rivera's estate. Separately, § 8850(c) requires the inventory to show, to the extent Morgan Lee can ascertain it, which portions of the property are community, quasi-community, and separate property of Pat Morgan Rivera.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The inventory and appraisal shall separately list each item and shall state the fair market value of the item at the time of the decedent’s death in monetary terms opposite the item."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8802 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8802 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8802.)
  "The inventory, including partial and supplemental inventories, shall include all property to be administered in the decedent’s estate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8850(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8850(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8850.)
  "The inventory shall show, to the extent ascertainable by the personal representative, the portions of the property that are community, quasi-community, and separate property of the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8850(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8850(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8850.)
  Known gap: This clause does not quote § 8850(b), which separately lists specific categories of property the inventory must particularly specify (money owed to the decedent, a decedent's partnership interest, and money and cash items as defined in § 8901) — it only notes that such a subdivision exists. It also does not address the Judicial Council's prescribed inventory-and-appraisal form (referenced in other Probate Code provisions this clause does not cite), which sets out the mechanical layout these statutory content requirements are filled into.

PROPERTY THE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE APPRAISES DIRECTLY
Probate Code § 8901 lists categories of property that the personal representative — rather than the probate referee — appraises, excluding any item whose fair market value is, in Morgan Lee's opinion, different from its face value. The listed categories include money and other cash items (defined as a check, draft, money order, or similar instrument issued on or before Pat Morgan Rivera's date of death that can be immediately converted to cash), certain checks issued after death, financial-institution accounts, cash deposits and money market mutual funds, and, separately, proceeds of life and accident insurance policies and of retirement plans and annuities payable on death in lump sum amounts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The personal representative shall appraise the following property, excluding items whose fair market value is, in the opinion of the personal representative, an amount different from the face value of the property: (a) Money and other cash items. As used in this subdivision, a “cash item” is a check, draft, money order, or similar instrument issued on or before the date of the decedent’s death that can be immediately converted to cash."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8901 intro & (a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8901(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8901.)
  "Proceeds of life and accident insurance policies and retirement plans and annuities payable on death in lump sum amounts."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8901(e) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8901(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8901.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the introductory clause together with subdivision (a) (cash items) and subdivision (e) (life insurance and retirement proceeds); it does not separately quote subdivisions (b), (c), or (d), which cover post-death checks, financial-institution accounts, and cash deposits or money market mutual funds, though the body text above summarizes them. The exclusion for items whose value the personal representative believes differs from face value is a judgment call the statute leaves to the personal representative's own opinion, and § 8901 does not itself define how that opinion is to be formed or documented.

DELIVERY OF THE INVENTORY TO THE REFEREE, AND THE REFEREE'S APPRAISAL OF REMAINING PROPERTY
Probate Code § 8902 requires the personal representative to deliver the inventory to the probate referee designated by the court, together with the supporting data the referee needs to appraise the property assigned to the referee, and requires the referee to appraise all property other than the property the personal representative appraises directly under § 8901. Section 8901(d) itself points forward to this division of labor: all mutual funds, stocks, bonds, and other securities other than cash deposits and money market mutual funds are, by that subdivision's own terms, to be appraised under §§ 8902 through 8909.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute: (a) The personal representative shall deliver the inventory to the probate referee designated by the court, together with necessary supporting data to enable the probate referee to make an appraisal of the property in the inventory to be appraised by the probate referee. (b) The probate referee shall appraise all property other than that appraised by the personal representative."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8902 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8902 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8902.)
  "All other mutual funds, stocks, bonds, and other securities shall be appraised pursuant to Sections 8902 to 8909, inclusive."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8901(d) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8901(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8901.)
  Known gap: Section 8902 begins with the qualifying phrase 'Except as otherwise provided by statute,' signaling that other Probate Code provisions — including a provision (not fetched or independently verified in this session) allowing an independent expert to appraise certain property under § 8904, which § 8961(a) elsewhere cross-references — can shift particular property outside this default personal-representative/referee split. This clause does not verify the text or scope of § 8904.

DUTY TO FILE A SUPPLEMENTAL INVENTORY AND APPRAISAL FOR LATER-DISCOVERED PROPERTY
Probate Code § 8801 provides that if the personal representative acquires knowledge of estate property that was not included in a prior inventory and appraisal, the personal representative must file a supplemental inventory and appraisal of that property, prepared in the manner prescribed for an original inventory and appraisal. That supplemental filing is due within four months after the personal representative acquires knowledge of the property, though the court may allow further time as is reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If the personal representative acquires knowledge of property to be administered in the decedent’s estate that is not included in a prior inventory and appraisal, the personal representative shall file a supplemental inventory and appraisal of the property in the manner prescribed for an original inventory and appraisal. The supplemental inventory and appraisal shall be filed within four months after the personal representative acquires knowledge of the property. The court may allow such further time for filing a supplemental inventory and appraisal as is reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8801 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8801 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8801.)
  Known gap: Section 8801 does not itself define what it means to 'acquire knowledge' of previously undisclosed property, or specify any particular standard a court applies in deciding whether an extension request is 'reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case' — the same reasonableness language used, and left equally undefined, in § 8800(b)'s original-filing deadline. This clause does not address how a supplemental filing interacts with an estate that has already closed.

HOW THE PROBATE REFEREE IS COMPENSATED
Probate Code § 8960(a) provides that the commission and expenses payable to a probate referee are paid from Pat Morgan Rivera's estate. Under § 8960(b), the referee may not withhold the appraisal pending payment of the commission and expenses, and must instead deliver the appraisal to the personal representative promptly upon completion. Section 8960(c) classifies the referee's commission and expenses as an expense of administration, entitled to the payment priority set out in § 11420, paid in the course of administration. As for the amount, § 8961(a) sets the commission at one-tenth of one percent of the total value of the property for each estate appraised, computed excluding property the personal representative appraised under § 8901 or an independent expert appraised under § 8904.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) The commission and expenses provided by this article as compensation for the services of the probate referee shall be paid from the estate. (b) The probate referee may not withhold the appraisal until the commission and expenses are paid, but shall deliver the appraisal to the personal representative promptly upon completion."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8960(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8960(a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8960.)
  "The commission and expenses of the probate referee are an expense of administration, entitled to the priority for payment provided by Section 11420, and shall be paid in the course of administration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8960(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8960(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8960.)
  "A commission of one-tenth of one percent of the total value of the property for each estate appraised, subject to Section 8963. The commission shall be computed excluding property appraised by the personal representative pursuant to Section 8901 or by an independent expert pursuant to Section 8904."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8961(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8961(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8961.)
  Known gap: Section 8961(a) states its one-tenth-of-one-percent commission is itself 'subject to Section 8963' — a separate section, not fetched or independently verified in this session, that (based on the cross-reference alone) appears to set some further limit on the commission; this clause does not state what that limit is. This clause also does not quote § 8961(b), which separately requires the referee to file a verified account of expenses with the inventory and appraisal, beyond noting that such a requirement exists.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet was reviewed on September 6, 2026, in Oakland, California. It states general facts about California's statutory inventory-and-appraisal procedure and probate-referee appointment provisions in the administration of Pat Morgan Rivera's estate before Superior Court of California in Alameda County, case number PRO-26-123456. It is not legal advice about any specific item of estate property, does not itself file any inventory and appraisal or select any probate referee, and does not extend, shorten, or waive any deadline this procedure imposes.
